tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for an 84-year-old resident in a long-term care facility. Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results, then read the skin assessment note. Click to highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.passage: 0915: {{4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood}}. {{Skin on both forearms thin and translucent}}, with {{flat purple patches on both forearms}}. {{Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks}}. {{Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration}}. Resident {{eats about 30–40% of meals}} and {{showers daily with hot water and deodorant soap}}. Resident is {{alert and oriented ×4}}.
optionRationales: Requires follow-up. An open, bleeding wound needs bleeding control, cleaning, and a dressing, and it is a portal for infection.
Does not require follow-up. Thin, translucent skin is an expected age-related change (fewer melanocytes, thinner layers), although it guides prevention.
Does not require follow-up. Flat purple patches from fragile vessels (senile purpura) are an expected finding in older adults.
Requires follow-up. Dry skin is common with aging, but scratch marks mean the skin barrier is broken and the itching needs treatment.
Does not require follow-up. Intact heels and sacrum are a normal finding.
Requires follow-up. Poor intake limits the calories, protein, and vitamins needed for healing. The albumin of 3.0 g/dL supports this concern.
Requires follow-up. Daily hot showers with harsh soap strip oils from aging skin. Older adults should bathe every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser.
Does not require follow-up. Full orientation is the resident's baseline.
questions.rationale: Many findings in older adult skin are expected: thin, translucent skin, senile purpura, and some dryness. The nurse separates these from findings that need action: an open, bleeding skin tear, broken skin from scratching, poor nutritional intake, and a bathing routine that damages fragile skin.
questions.takeaway: Thin skin and senile purpura are expected with aging. Open wounds, scratching, poor intake, and harsh bathing need action.
questions.hintContent: Recall the normal skin changes of aging, then look for findings that break the skin or slow healing.
questions.hintStrategy: Go through each segment and ask whether it is expected for an 84-year-old or whether it is harming the skin now. Highlight only findings that need action.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

Day 1, 0915 skin assessment: 4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood. Both forearms thin and translucent with flat purple patches. Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks. Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. For each finding, indicate whether it is likely to delay healing of the resident's skin tear or is not likely to delay healing.
optionRationales: Likely to delay healing. Albumin below 3.5 g/dL signals poor nutrition, a higher infection risk, and delayed healing.
Likely to delay healing. Low hemoglobin means less oxygen is delivered to the healing tissue.
Likely to delay healing. Diabetes is a chronic illness that increases skin risk, and high glucose slows healing.
Likely to delay healing. Healing needs extra calories, protein, and vitamins A and C, which poor intake does not supply.
Not likely to delay healing. A normal WBC means infection defense is adequate.
Not likely to delay healing. A normal platelet count means clotting is adequate.
questions.rationale: Labs that affect wound healing include WBC (infection defense), hemoglobin (oxygen delivery), coagulation, and albumin (nutrition). This resident has low albumin, low hemoglobin, high glucose, and poor intake, all of which slow healing. The normal WBC and platelets are reassuring.
questions.takeaway: Low albumin, low hemoglobin, high glucose, and poor intake all slow healing.
questions.hintContent: Recall what each lab tells you about oxygen delivery, infection defense, clotting, and nutrition.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each value with its reference range first. Then ask how the abnormal ones affect new tissue growth.

Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

Day 1, 0915 skin assessment: 4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood. Both forearms thin and translucent with flat purple patches. Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks. Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The resident is at highest risk for {0} because of {1}. Healing of any new injury is most likely to be slowed by {2}.

options: new skin tears and bruising
allergic contact dermatitis
melanoma
a fungal infection between the toes
thin skin with fragile vessels and less subcutaneous cushioning
an SpO₂ of 96% on room air
a normal white blood cell count
full orientation to person, place, and time
poor intake with an albumin of 3.0 g/dL
a platelet count of 210,000/mm³
a temperature of 36.4 °C (97.5 °F)
her use of a wheelchair for long distances

questions.rationale: Aging skin is thinner and less elastic, with fragile vessels (senile purpura) and less subcutaneous fat for cushioning. Older adults therefore have a higher injury risk and slower healing. Poor intake with albumin below 3.5 g/dL adds to delayed healing and infection risk.
questions.takeaway: Thin skin + fragile vessels + less fat = injury risk. Low albumin = slow healing.
questions.hintContent: Recall the functional skin changes of aging (↑ injury risk, ↑ healing time) and which lab signals poor nutrition.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the problem the most cues support. Each reason you pick must directly explain the problem you chose.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

Day 1, 0915 skin assessment: 4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood. Both forearms thin and translucent with flat purple patches. Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks. Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. The nurse is planning care to protect the resident's skin and promote healing. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Pad the wheelchair armrests and use a draw sheet with two staff to reposition the resident
Encourage the resident to wear long-sleeved clothing
Secure the forearm dressing with standard adhesive tape so it stays in place
Request a dietitian consult for more calories, protein, and vitamins A and C
Perform hand hygiene before and after dressing changes and discard soiled dressings safely
Pull the resident up in bed by the arms to avoid pressure on the sacrum
optionRationales: Correct. Padding and lifting with a draw sheet prevent friction and bumps that tear fragile skin.
Correct. Long sleeves protect thin forearm skin from bumps and scrapes.
Incorrect. Removing adhesive tape can tear fragile older adult skin. Use a nonadherent dressing held with a wrap or tape-free product.
Correct. Healing needs extra calories, protein, and vitamins A and C, and a dietitian can plan supplements or small frequent meals.
Correct. Hand hygiene before and after wound care and safe disposal of soiled dressings prevent infection.
Incorrect. Pulling on the arms causes friction and skin tears. The resident should be lifted with a draw sheet, never dragged.
questions.rationale: Older adults have an increased injury risk and slower healing. The plan protects fragile skin (padding, draw sheets, long sleeves, no adhesive tape), supports healing with nutrition, and prevents infection with hand hygiene and safe dressing disposal.
questions.takeaway: Pad, lift, cover, no tape, feed, and clean hands.
questions.hintContent: Recall how friction, adhesives, and poor nutrition affect thin, aging skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option on its own. Eliminate anything that adds friction or pulls on fragile skin.

tabs.html:
Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

Day 1, 0915 skin assessment: 4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood. Both forearms thin and translucent with flat purple patches. Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks. Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration. Alert and oriented ×4.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes. The nurse goes to the resident's room to care for the skin tear. After performing hand hygiene and putting on gloves, which action should the nurse take first?
options: Clean the skin tear with normal saline
Cover the skin tear with a nonadherent dressing and a wrap
Apply gentle pressure with gauze and elevate the arm
Complete an incident report about the transfer
optionRationales: Cleaning with saline prevents infection, but it comes after the bleeding is controlled.
A dressing is applied after bleeding is controlled and the wound is cleaned.
Correct. In acute wound care, bleeding is controlled first with pressure and elevation. Pressure is gentle because the skin is fragile.
The event should be documented and reported, but only after the resident's wound has been cared for.
questions.rationale: Care of an untreated acute wound follows a sequence: control bleeding with pressure and elevation, then prevent infection by cleaning with normal saline and covering with a dressing, then manage pain and swelling and assess for shock. Documentation follows direct care.
questions.takeaway: Acute wound: pressure and elevate → clean with saline → cover.
questions.hintContent: Recall the order of acute wound care for an untreated wound.
questions.hintStrategy: All of these actions will be done. Choose the one that must happen before the others can be done safely.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Day 1, 0900 (Long-term care): 84-year-old resident with type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, admitted to the facility 2 weeks ago after a fall at home. Uses a wheelchair for distances. The UAP reports that the resident “bumped her arm on the wheelchair armrest” during a transfer. Resident says, “My skin tears and bruises if you just look at it.” Has showered daily with hot water and deodorant soap “my whole life.” Eats about 30–40% of meals. Usually wears short-sleeved shirts.

Day 1, 0915 skin assessment: 4-cm open skin tear on the left forearm, oozing bright red blood. Both forearms thin and translucent with flat purple patches. Lower legs dry and flaky with scratch marks. Heels and sacrum intact without discoloration. Alert and oriented ×4.

Day 14, 1000: Skin tear on the left forearm closed, with no drainage or redness. Wheelchair armrests are padded, and the resident wears long sleeves. Lower legs soft and moisturized, with no new scratch marks. Now showers every other day with lukewarm water and a mild cleanser. Eats about 40% of meals and often refuses the supplement. A new bruise on the right upper arm; the resident says, “The new aide pulled me up in bed by my arms last night.”

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results for day 14. For each finding, indicate whether the plan of care has been effective or not effective.
rows: Skin tear closed with no drainage or redness
Lower legs soft, with no new scratch marks
Eats about 40% of meals; albumin 3.1 g/dL
New bruise after being pulled up in bed by the arms
No new injuries on the padded forearms
optionRationales: Effective. The wound healed without signs of infection.
Effective. Gentler bathing and moisturizing have restored the skin barrier.
Not effective. Intake is still poor and albumin is still below 3.5 g/dL. The nutrition plan needs to be revised with the dietitian.
Not effective. Staff are still using a technique that injures fragile skin. The nurse needs to reinforce draw-sheet use with all UAPs.
Effective. Padding and long sleeves are preventing new skin tears.
questions.rationale: Evaluation looks at each goal separately. Skin protection, bathing changes, and wound care worked. Nutrition has not improved, and a new injury shows that safe lifting is not being used by all staff, so those parts of the plan need to be revised.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate each goal on its own. One success does not mean the whole plan worked.
questions.hintContent: Compare each day-14 finding with the day-1 baseline and with the goals of protecting skin and promoting healing.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, ask whether the finding moved toward the goal. Don't let the overall improvement hide findings that did not change.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Clinic, 1015: 38-year-old client reports an intensely itchy rash that started 2 days after dyeing her hair at home with a new permanent hair dye. She used a different dye of the same color 3 months ago and had mild itching afterward. Assessment: red, swollen skin with small vesicles along the hairline, forehead, tops of the ears, and back of the neck, ending sharply where the dye touched the skin. No crusting or drainage. No lesions elsewhere. Denies shortness of breath or throat tightness. No one at home has a rash.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Allergic contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis
Impetigo
Head lice
Teach the client to avoid the hair dye and document the allergy
Place the client on contact precautions
Apply cool compresses and the prescribed topical corticosteroid
Apply an antifungal cream to the rash twice daily
Cover the rash with an occlusive dressing overnight
Intensity of itching
Serum albumin level
Wound culture results
Extent of redness and vesicles
Nasal culture results

condition: Correct. An itchy rash with vesicles that appears at the site of contact, takes the shape of the exposure, and follows an earlier sensitizing exposure is allergic contact dermatitis. Dyes are a common allergen.
Irritant dermatitis is direct chemical damage that causes red, dry, cracked, burning skin. It does not need a prior exposure, and vesicles in a sharp pattern after re-exposure point to an allergy.
Impetigo causes honey-colored crusts and is contagious. This rash has no crusts, and no one at home is affected.
Head lice cause scalp itching with nits on the hair shafts, not a vesicular rash that ends where dye touched the skin.
actions: Correct. Avoiding the allergen is the main treatment, and documenting it prevents future exposure.
Contact dermatitis is not contagious, so isolation is not needed.
Correct. Cool compresses soothe itching, and a prescribed topical corticosteroid reduces the inflammation.
This rash is not fungal, so an antifungal will not help.
Occlusion traps heat and moisture and increases absorption of topical drugs. It is used only when prescribed.
parameters: Correct. Less itching shows the inflammation is settling.
Albumin reflects nutritional status, not the course of dermatitis.
This is not an infected wound, so no culture has been ordered.
Correct. Shrinking redness and drying vesicles show the rash is resolving.
Nasal cultures are carrier studies for repeated bacterial infections, which do not apply here.

questions.rationale: Allergic contact dermatitis is an immune reaction that needs prior exposure. The rash appears at the allergen site, is shaped like the exposure, and may form vesicles or wheals. Dyes, perfumes, metals, latex, and poison plants are common allergens. Care is avoiding the allergen, soothing the skin, and using prescribed topical corticosteroids. Progress is shown by less itching and a shrinking rash.
questions.takeaway: Rash shaped like the exposure after prior contact = allergic contact dermatitis. Avoid, soothe, treat, and monitor the itch and rash.
questions.hintContent: Look at where the rash is, its shape, and whether the client had used a similar product before.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first. Then choose only the actions and parameters that fit that condition.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

tabs.title: History
tabs.html: 84-year-old client with hypertension and osteoarthritis. Lives with an adult son who is the primary caregiver. Medications: amlodipine, acetaminophen PRN. Home health nurse's first visit.

questions.stem: The home health nurse is performing a skin assessment. Refer to the History, then read the skin assessment note. Click to highlight the findings that require follow-up.
questions.passage: Skin on the backs of both hands is {{thin and translucent with visible veins}}. {{Flat, dark purple patches on the backs of both forearms}}; client says they appear “with the smallest bump.” {{Several oval bruises in different shades of purple, green, and yellow on both inner upper arms}}. {{Dry, flaky skin on both lower legs}}. {{Multiple waxy, brown, “stuck-on” raised lesions on the back}}. {{Small, bright red papules scattered on the trunk}}. A {{9-mm dark mole on the left calf with a notched, irregular border}} that the client says “seems bigger.” {{A pearly sore on the right ear rim that has bled on and off for 2 months}}.
optionRationales: Expected. Loss of dermal collagen and subcutaneous fat makes older adult skin thin and translucent.
Expected. Senile (actinic) purpura on the dorsal forearms comes from fragile dermal vessels in sun-damaged skin.
Requires follow-up. Bruises in different stages of healing on the protected inner upper arms fit a pattern of being grabbed. The nurse should assess further for elder abuse and report as required.
Expected. Fewer, less active sebaceous and sweat glands cause xerosis in older adults.
Expected. Seborrheic keratoses are benign, waxy, stuck-on lesions that are very common with aging.
Expected. Cherry angiomas are benign vascular papules that increase with age.
Requires follow-up. A mole that is asymmetric, has an irregular border, is > 6 mm, and is evolving meets several ABCDE criteria for melanoma.
Requires follow-up. A pearly lesion that bleeds and does not heal on a sun-exposed area suggests basal cell carcinoma and needs referral.
questions.rationale: Many skin changes are normal with aging: thinning, xerosis, senile purpura, seborrheic keratoses, and cherry angiomas. The nurse must tell these apart from findings that suggest harm or cancer. Patterned bruises of different ages on protected areas raise concern for abuse. An evolving, irregular mole and a nonhealing, bleeding lesion on the ear need prompt referral for evaluation for skin cancer.
questions.takeaway: Know normal aging skin so that you can recognize what is not normal: patterned bruises, evolving moles, and sores that do not heal.
questions.hintContent: Recall normal older adult skin findings (thinning, xerosis, senile purpura, benign growths), the ABCDE rule, and the typical location of accidental versus inflicted bruises.
questions.hintStrategy: For each segment, ask whether it is an expected age-related change or a sign of harm or disease. Also note where each bruise is located.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Wound Care (Acute Settings)
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 45-year-old client is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after falling through a glass door. A pressure dressing has been applied to a deep laceration on the right forearm. Read the nurse's assessment note. Click to highlight the findings that suggest the client may be developing shock.
questions.passage: Client is {{restless and keeps asking for water}}. {{Pulse 128/min and weak}}. {{Skin cool and clammy}}. {{BP 86/54 mm Hg}}. {{Small abrasions on both knees with a small amount of serous oozing}}. {{Pain 5/10 at the forearm laceration}}. {{SpO₂ 97% on room air}}. {{Closed, swollen bruise on the right hip}}.
optionRationales: Suggests shock. Restlessness and thirst are early signs of reduced blood volume and brain perfusion.
Suggests shock. A rapid, weak pulse is the body's attempt to maintain cardiac output after blood loss.
Suggests shock. Cool, clammy skin reflects vasoconstriction as blood is shunted to vital organs.
Suggests shock. Low blood pressure is a key sign of shock after bleeding.
Does not suggest shock. Minor serous oozing from superficial abrasions is expected.
Does not suggest shock. Moderate pain at the wound is expected and should be treated, but it is not a shock sign.
Does not suggest shock. Oxygen saturation is normal.
Does not suggest shock by itself. A closed wound (contusion) should be monitored, but it does not indicate shock.
questions.rationale: For untreated wounds, the nurse controls bleeding, prevents infection, manages pain and swelling, and assesses for shock: rapid pulse, cool clammy skin, and low BP, often with restlessness and thirst. These findings need immediate reporting and intervention.
questions.takeaway: Shock after a wound: rapid pulse, cool clammy skin, low BP, restlessness.
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs of shock listed for untreated acute wounds.
questions.hintStrategy: For each segment, ask whether it reflects the circulation failing or is an expected finding of a minor wound.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The clinic nurse is reviewing four clients' histories during intake. Which client should the nurse identify as having the greatest risk for vitamin D deficiency related to reduced skin synthesis?
options: A 24-year-old outdoor lifeguard with light skin who uses SPF 30 sunscreen
A 45-year-old landscaper with medium skin who works outside year-round
An 86-year-old homebound client with dark skin who rarely goes outdoors
A 16-year-old soccer player with dark skin who practices outdoors daily
optionRationales: Regular sun exposure lets the skin synthesize vitamin D, even with sunscreen in real-world use.
Year-round outdoor work gives frequent UV exposure for vitamin D synthesis.

Correct. The skin makes vitamin D when exposed to UVB. Several factors add up here: aging skin makes less vitamin D precursor, melanin reduces UVB absorption, and being homebound means little sun exposure.
Darker skin needs more UV exposure, but daily outdoor practice gives this adolescent enough sun.
questions.rationale: Vitamin D synthesis is a key skin function. It depends on UVB reaching the epidermis. Older age (less 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin), more melanin, and limited sun exposure each lower production, and this client has all three.
questions.takeaway: Older age + dark skin + homebound = triple risk for low vitamin D.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the skin needs in order to make vitamin D and what reduces that process.
questions.hintStrategy: Count the risk factors for each client. The best answer usually has several that add up.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Functions of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse has taught a client with diabetic peripheral neuropathy how to protect the skin of the feet. Monofilament testing shows absent sensation on both soles. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I will look at the bottoms of my feet with a mirror every night.”
“I will wear shoes or slippers even when I'm inside the house.”
“I will shake out my shoes and feel inside them before I put them on.”
“I will test my bath water by dipping my foot in before I get in.”
optionRationales: Correct practice. Daily visual inspection makes up for the lost protective sensation.
Correct practice. Footwear protects insensate feet from unnoticed trauma.
Correct practice. The client may not feel a pebble or rough seam, so the client checks shoes by hand or by looking.
Needs further teaching. A foot without sensation cannot detect dangerous heat. The client should test water with a thermometer or an elbow to avoid burns.
questions.rationale: Sensation is a protective function of the skin. When neuropathy removes it, the client must replace feeling with looking and with testing by another body part or a device. Using the numb foot to test water temperature risks a serious burn.
questions.takeaway: No feeling in the feet? Use eyes, hands, and a thermometer, not the feet.
questions.hintContent: Recall which skin function the dermal nerve endings serve and what happens when neuropathy destroys them.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a negatively worded item. Look for the unsafe statement.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Functions of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing several clients' problems related to impaired skin function. For each client finding, indicate which skin function is primarily impaired.
rows: A client with extensive open abrasions from a motorcycle crash develops a wound infection
An 88-year-old client with little subcutaneous fat shivers in a room that feels comfortable to staff
A client with a spinal cord injury does not notice a hot beverage spilled on the lap
A client with widespread blistering skin loss becomes hypothermic after a dressing change
A client with diabetic neuropathy does not notice a blister from new shoes
optionRationales: Protection. Intact skin is the barrier against microorganisms, and the abrasions breached it.
Temperature regulation. Loss of subcutaneous fat with aging impairs heat conservation.
Sensation. Loss of sensory input from the skin below the injury removes the warning signal for pain and heat.
Temperature regulation. Without intact skin, heat is lost from exposed surfaces, especially during wound care.
Sensation. Neuropathy removes the feeling of pressure and pain, so injuries go unnoticed.
questions.rationale: The skin protects against pathogens and trauma, regulates temperature through blood vessels, sweat glands, and subcutaneous insulation, and gives sensation through dermal receptors. Naming which function has failed guides the nursing action: infection prevention, warming, or protection from injury the client cannot feel.
questions.takeaway: Match the failure to the function: infection = barrier, cold or heat = regulation, unnoticed injury = sensation.
questions.hintContent: Review the main skin functions and the layer that performs each.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, ask what went wrong for the client (infection, temperature, or feeling) rather than what caused it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Layers of the Skin
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with COPD has taken prednisone 20 mg PO daily for 2 years. The nurse notes thin, shiny skin on the forearms with several purple bruises and a healing skin tear. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: These skin changes are most likely caused by {0}, which reduces {1} in the dermis. The client is at highest risk for {2}.

options: long-term corticosteroid therapy
chronic hypoxemia
vitamin C toxicity
hypothyroidism
collagen formation
melanin production
keratin production
sebum secretion
new skin tears
keloid formation
melasma
psoriatic plaques

questions.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids inhibit fibroblasts and collagen synthesis. This causes dermal atrophy, fragile capillaries (steroid purpura), and poor wound healing. Thin skin with weak dermal support tears easily with shearing or friction, so the nurse uses gentle handling, lift sheets, padding, and no adhesive tape.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids thin the dermis, so handle the skin like tissue paper.
questions.hintContent: The dermis gets its strength from a structural protein made by fibroblasts. Recall which medication class suppresses them.
questions.hintStrategy: Complete the blanks in order. The first answer (the cause) should explain the second (the mechanism) and the third (the risk).

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Cultural Considerations in Skin Assessment
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client with deeply pigmented skin is admitted with suspected hepatitis. Total bilirubin is 4.8 mg/dL. The nurse notes a slight yellowish tint at the outer edges of the sclera. Which assessment should the nurse perform next to confirm jaundice?
options: Press on the nail beds and time the capillary refill
Inspect the hard palate and the palms of the hands
Inspect the lower eyelid conjunctiva for pallor
Compare the skin color on the chest with the forearms
optionRationales: Capillary refill assesses peripheral perfusion, not jaundice.

Correct. In dark skin, the sclera can normally look yellowish at the edges from subconjunctival fat, and carotene can tint the skin. Yellow on the hard palate, palms, and soles confirms jaundice more reliably.
The conjunctiva is assessed for pallor (anemia), not jaundice.
Jaundice is hard to see in deeply pigmented skin, so general skin color is not a reliable indicator.
questions.rationale: In deeply pigmented skin, assess color changes where melanin is minimal. For jaundice, the best sites are the hard palate, palms, and soles, along with the center of the sclera. Pallor is best seen in the conjunctiva and mucosa, and cyanosis in the lips, nail beds, and buccal mucosa.
questions.takeaway: Jaundice in dark skin: check the hard palate, palms, and soles, not just the sclera.
questions.hintContent: Recall where melanin is thinnest and why peripheral sclera can be misleading in darker skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate the options that assess a different color change (perfusion, pallor) than the one in the stem.

questions.stem: The nurse receives hand-off report on four clients with skin findings. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with psoriasis who has silvery, scaly plaques on both elbows
An older adult with several waxy, stuck-on brown papules on the upper back
An adolescent with scattered pustules on the forehead and chin
A client with new raised wheals on the trunk who reports a hoarse voice
optionRationales: Chronic, stable psoriatic plaques are not an immediate threat.
Seborrheic keratoses are benign age-related lesions.
Acne vulgaris is common in adolescents and is not urgent.
Correct. Wheals (urticaria) with a new hoarse voice suggest a systemic allergic reaction with possible laryngeal edema. This is an airway threat that needs immediate assessment.
questions.rationale: Most skin lesions are chronic or benign. When a skin finding comes with airway symptoms, the client moves to the top of the list. Hoarseness with wheals suggests angioedema of the larynx or early anaphylaxis. Airway comes first.
questions.takeaway: Wheals + a voice change = airway emergency, not a skin problem.
questions.hintContent: Recall what primary lesion a wheal is and what systemic process it can signal.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the ABCs. Look for any option that includes a cue beyond the skin that threatens the airway, breathing, or circulation.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Skin Lesions
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client comes to the clinic with a rash on the torso that began 4 days ago. Which data should the nurse collect during the focused skin assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Size of representative lesions measured in millimeters or centimeters
Distribution and arrangement of the lesions (for example, linear, clustered, or scattered)
Any new medications, soaps, foods, or exposures before the rash appeared
The content of a pustule obtained by squeezing it onto gauze
Associated symptoms such as itching, pain, or fever
The likely diagnosis based on the appearance of the rash
optionRationales: Correct. Measured, objective dimensions let the team trend changes over time.
Correct. The pattern and distribution (for example, clustered vesicles or linear streaks from poison ivy) are major clues to the cause.
Correct. A history of new drugs, products, and exposures helps identify allergic, irritant, and drug reactions.
Incorrect. Squeezing a lesion injures tissue and can spread infection. A culture, if needed, is collected by swab per protocol.
Correct. Subjective symptoms (pruritus, pain, systemic signs) guide the differential and the priority.
Incorrect. The nurse describes and documents findings. Making the medical diagnosis is outside RN scope.
questions.rationale: A complete focused skin assessment includes objective lesion data (type, size, color, shape, arrangement, distribution, exudate), subjective data (onset, symptoms), and history (medications, exposures, contacts). The nurse documents precisely and avoids harmful techniques and medical diagnosis.
questions.takeaway: Describe, measure, map, and ask what changed. Don't squeeze, and don't diagnose.
questions.hintContent: Recall the elements of a lesion description and the history questions that point to the cause of a rash.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option on its own: is it within RN scope, safe, and useful for describing the rash?

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Diagnostic Tests
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with several sharply demarcated, milky-white patches on the hands and around the mouth is scheduled for a Wood lamp examination to evaluate for vitiligo. Which instruction should the nurse give the client before the examination?
options: “Do not eat or drink anything for 8 hours before the examination.”
“A small skin sample will be removed after a local anesthetic injection.”
“Do not apply lotion, makeup, or creams to your hands and face that day.”
“The lamp will be pressed against your skin in a brightly lit exam room.”
optionRationales: A Wood lamp examination is an external, noninvasive light test. No fasting is required.
The Wood lamp does not remove tissue. A biopsy is a separate test used to tell benign from malignant lesions.
Correct. Many lotions, cosmetics, deodorants, and medicated creams fluoresce under ultraviolet light and can cause false results, so the skin should be clean and free of products.
The exam is done in a darkened room with the lamp held about 10–13 cm (4–5 inches) from the skin, not touching it.
questions.rationale: A Wood lamp emits long-wave ultraviolet light in a darkened room. Depigmented skin in vitiligo appears bright blue-white, and some fungal and bacterial infections fluoresce in characteristic colors. The test is painless and noninvasive. Topical products can fluoresce and distort the results, so the client comes with clean skin, and the client avoids looking directly into the light.
questions.takeaway: Wood lamp: darkened room, UV light held away from the skin, no creams or makeup beforehand.
questions.hintContent: Recall what a Wood lamp is, how it is used, and what could make the skin glow falsely under ultraviolet light.
questions.hintStrategy: Picture the test being performed. Eliminate options that describe a different kind of procedure, then choose the instruction that protects the accuracy of the result.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A 6-year-old admitted for asthma is found to have honey-crusted lesions on the chin that are diagnosed as impetigo. A topical antibiotic is started today. Which infection control measure should the nurse implement?
options: Contact precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy begins
Droplet precautions until all of the crusted lesions have fully healed
Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room for 48 hours
Standard precautions only, with the lesions left open to air
optionRationales: Correct. Impetigo requires contact precautions until 24 hours after effective therapy is started.
Impetigo spreads by direct contact, not droplets.
Impetigo is not airborne.
Standard precautions alone do not prevent spread of this highly contagious bacterial skin infection in a hospital.
questions.rationale: Impetigo is a bacterial infection that spreads by direct contact with lesions or contaminated items. Contact precautions (gown and gloves) continue until 24 hours after effective treatment begins. The same rule applies to children returning to school or daycare.
questions.takeaway: Impetigo = contact precautions until 24 hours of effective therapy.
questions.hintContent: Recall how impetigo is spread and the rule for when the child is no longer contagious.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the route of transmission to the type of precaution. Then check that the duration also fits.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: In a long-term care facility, a resident is diagnosed with scabies, and two staff members who provided care report new itching. The charge nurse is coordinating the facility's response. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Place the resident on contact precautions with gown and gloves for all direct care
Arrange for the resident, exposed residents, and exposed staff to be treated at the same time
Machine-wash the resident's bedding and clothing used in the past 3 days in hot water and dry on high heat
Remove precautions as soon as the resident reports that the itching has stopped
Seal items that cannot be washed in a plastic bag for at least 72 hours
Apply permethrin cream only to the areas where burrows are visible
optionRationales: Correct. Scabies spreads by close skin-to-skin contact and contaminated linens, so gown and gloves are used for direct care.
Correct. Treating all close contacts at the same time prevents passing the mites back and forth.
Correct. Hot washing and high-heat drying of recently used items kills mites and eggs.
Incorrect. Itching can continue for weeks after successful treatment, so it is not a guide for stopping precautions.
Correct. Mites cannot survive more than a few days away from human skin, so bagging items that can't be washed kills them.
Incorrect. Scabicide is applied to all skin from the neck down, because mites are present beyond the visible burrows.
questions.rationale: Scabies is a parasitic infection spread by close contact and shared items. Controlling an outbreak needs contact precautions, treatment of the resident and all contacts at the same time, laundering or bagging of personal items, and whole-body application of the prescribed treatment.
questions.takeaway: Scabies: treat everyone at once, neck to toes. Hot-wash or bag items. Itching can last weeks.
questions.hintContent: Recall how scabies spreads between people and through shared items.
questions.hintStrategy: Each option is a separate true/false statement. Check each for timing (how long) and extent (how much skin).

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical-surgical unit is reviewing four clients with skin and wound findings. Which client's findings require the nurse's immediate attention?
options: A client with athlete's foot who reports itching and scaling between the toes
A client with psoriasis who has silvery, scaly plaques on both elbows and both knees
A client whose incision has new purulent drainage and a fever of 38.9 °C (102 °F)
A client with a knee abrasion that has a small amount of clear, serous oozing
optionRationales: Athlete's foot is a common fungal infection. It needs treatment and teaching, but it is not urgent.
Silvery plaques are the expected lesions of chronic psoriasis.
Correct. Purulent drainage, spreading redness, and fever are signs of wound infection that is spreading. This client needs prompt assessment, a wound culture, and notification of the provider.
A small amount of serous oozing from a partial-thickness abrasion is expected.
questions.rationale: Most skin findings are stable or chronic. Signs of wound infection (redness, swelling, purulent drainage, necrosis) with fever mean the infection is progressing and require immediate follow-up. Wound cultures confirm the infection and guide antibiotic choice.
questions.takeaway: Purulent drainage + spreading redness + fever = act now.
questions.hintContent: Recall the signs of wound infection and which findings are expected with chronic or minor skin conditions.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify which findings are expected for each condition. The client whose findings are unexpected and getting worse comes first.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 35-year-old client who runs daily is diagnosed with tinea pedis and prescribed a topical antifungal cream. Which instructions should the nurse include in the teaching plan? Select all that apply.
options: Dry thoroughly between the toes after bathing
Wear cotton or moisture-wicking socks and change them when damp
Stop the cream as soon as the itching goes away
Wear sandals or shower shoes in locker rooms and public showers
Rotate athletic shoes so each pair can dry out between uses
Share towels only with members of the same household
optionRationales: Correct. Dermatophytes thrive in warm, moist spaces, so drying between the toes removes that environment.
Correct. Keeping the feet dry reduces fungal growth.
Incorrect. Stopping early leads to relapse. The client continues the full prescribed course, often 1–2 weeks after symptoms clear.
Correct. Footwear in communal wet areas reduces exposure and spread.
Correct. Shoes need to dry out to reduce the fungal load.
Incorrect. Tinea spreads through shared towels and is common within households, so towels should not be shared.
questions.rationale: Tinea pedis is a dermatophyte infection that is promoted by warmth, moisture, and occlusion. Teaching focuses on keeping the feet dry, protective footwear, not sharing personal items, and completing the full antifungal course.
questions.takeaway: Fungus loves warm, wet, and dark. Keep feet dry, don't share, and finish the course.
questions.hintContent: Recall the environment dermatophytes need to grow and how they spread between people.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it makes the foot drier or reduces spread. Watch for options that stop treatment early.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infection Prevention, Exercise, & Nutrition
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A client has a draining infected wound on the thigh and is on contact precautions. The nurse is changing the dressing. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Perform hand hygiene, then put on a gown and clean gloves before entering
Remove the soiled dressing and discard it with the gloves in a leak-proof bag
Perform hand hygiene and put on a new pair of gloves
Cleanse the wound with normal saline, moving from the center outward
Apply the new dressing and label it with the date, time, and initials
questions.rationale: PPE goes on before contact (hand hygiene, then gown, then gloves). The soiled dressing is removed and discarded safely with the dirty gloves. Hand hygiene is repeated with fresh gloves before touching the wound. The wound is cleansed with saline from the least contaminated area (center) outward, and then a clean dressing is applied and labeled.
questions.takeaway: Hand hygiene before and after wound care. Clean gloves after the dirty dressing. Clean from the center outward.
questions.hintContent: Separate the dirty part of the procedure (removing the old dressing) from the clean part (wound care), and think about what must happen between them.
questions.hintStrategy: Order the steps to protect yourself first, then to never move from dirty to clean without a glove change and hand hygiene.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Infectious Skin Disorders
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing four clients who each have tinea (a fungal skin infection). Which client is at greatest risk for a serious complication from the fungal infection?
options: A 20-year-old college athlete with athlete's foot
A 35-year-old with ringworm on the forearm after adopting a kitten
A 58-year-old receiving chemotherapy for leukemia
A 10-year-old with a scaly patch on the scalp
optionRationales: Athlete's foot in a healthy young adult is common and usually responds to topical treatment.
Ringworm in a healthy adult is usually a minor, local infection.
Correct. Fungal infections are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients. Chemotherapy weakens the immune system, so the infection can spread or become severe.
Tinea is common in children and needs treatment, but a healthy child is not at the highest risk for serious complications.
questions.rationale: Fungal infections are common and usually minor, but they are more dangerous in immunocompromised clients, such as clients receiving chemotherapy. These clients need close monitoring and early treatment.
questions.takeaway: Fungal skin infections are most dangerous in immunocompromised clients.
questions.hintContent: Recall which clients the slides identify as most endangered by fungal infections.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the client whose immune defenses are weakest.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Lifespan Considerations – Infants and Children
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The pediatric clinic nurse has taught several parents about their children's skin infections. For each parent statement, indicate whether it shows understanding of the teaching or a need for further teaching.
rows: “My child with chickenpox can go back to child care once every blister has crusted over.”
“My son shouldn't pick at or bite the warts on his fingers, because that can spread them.”
“I'll give my daughter aspirin to bring down the fever from her chickenpox.”
“I'll keep my child's fingernails short so scratching doesn't spread the impetigo.”
“After the first lice treatment, I won't need to check my child's hair again.”
optionRationales: Indicates understanding. Varicella is contagious until all lesions are dry and crusted, which is when the child can return to child care or school.
Indicates understanding. Common warts are caused by human papillomavirus and spread by autoinoculation from picking, biting, or shaving over them.

Needs further teaching. Aspirin and other salicylates given to children with varicella or influenza are linked to Reye syndrome (acute encephalopathy and liver failure). Acetaminophen is used for fever instead.
Indicates understanding. Scratching carries bacteria from impetigo lesions to other skin. Short nails and covering lesions reduce autoinoculation.
Needs further teaching. Pediculicides do not kill all eggs. Hair is checked with a nit comb every 2–3 days, and a second treatment is usually given about 9 days later if live lice are found.
questions.rationale: Evaluating teaching about childhood skin infections focuses on how each infection spreads, when the child is no longer contagious, and safe symptom management. Varicella is contagious until all lesions crust, warts and impetigo spread by autoinoculation, lice need follow-up combing and often retreatment, and salicylates are avoided in children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.
questions.takeaway: Chickenpox: crusted = back to school, and no aspirin. Warts and impetigo spread by scratching. Lice need a recheck and often a second treatment.
questions.hintContent: Recall how varicella, warts, impetigo, and lice spread, when each stops being contagious, and which fever reducer is avoided in children with viral illnesses.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each row on its own. Ask whether the parent's plan would keep the child and others safe if it were followed exactly.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Contact Dermatitis
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client has linear streaks of itchy vesicles on both forearms 2 days after clearing brush and poison ivy from a yard. After teaching, which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “If I scratch open these blisters, the fluid will spread the rash.”
“I should wash the gloves and clothes I wore in the yard.”
“Cool compresses and calamine can help calm the itching.”
“Next time I'll wash my skin with soap and water as soon as I finish yard work.”
optionRationales: Needs further teaching. Blister fluid does not spread the rash. New areas appear from delayed reactions or from oil still on the skin, clothing, tools, or pets. Scratching should still be avoided because it can cause infection.
Correct statement. The plant oil stays on clothing, gloves, and tools and can cause new exposures until they are washed.
Correct statement. Cool compresses, calamine, and oatmeal baths relieve itching.
Correct statement. Washing within minutes to a few hours can remove the oil before it binds to the skin.
questions.rationale: Poison ivy causes allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed immune reaction to the plant's oil. The rash often forms linear streaks where the plant brushed the skin. It is not contagious, and vesicle fluid does not spread it. Teaching focuses on removing the oil from skin and objects, relieving symptoms, and avoiding the plant.
questions.takeaway: Poison ivy spreads through the oil, not the blister fluid. Wash skin, clothes, and tools.
questions.hintContent: Recall what substance in the plant causes the reaction and where it can remain after exposure.
questions.hintStrategy: Negatively worded item: look for the one statement that is factually incorrect.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Genetic Considerations & Risk Factors
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse at a community health fair is screening clients for risk of skin disorders. Which clients have an increased risk? Select all that apply.
options: A 79-year-old whose skin has become thin and heals slowly
A 30-year-old whose parent and sibling have a genetic skin condition
A 55-year-old who has taken oral steroids for 2 years
A 40-year-old with poor nutrition and recent weight loss
A 25-year-old who eats a balanced diet and moisturizes daily
A 35-year-old who uses a mild cleanser and wears sunscreen daily
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults have thinner skin and slower healing.
Correct. Genetics and family history increase the risk of skin disorders.
Correct. Medications such as steroids can thin the skin.
Correct. Poor nutrition causes skin changes and delayed healing.
Incorrect. Good nutrition and moisturizing protect the skin.
Incorrect. Mild cleansers and sunscreen are protective habits.
questions.rationale: Risk factors for skin disorders include genetics and family history, older age (thinner skin, slower healing), medications (steroids, antibiotics, chemotherapy, antifungals), chronic illness, and poor nutrition. Protective habits include good nutrition, moisturizing, mild cleansers, and sun protection.
questions.takeaway: Genetics, age, medications, chronic illness, and poor nutrition raise skin risk.
questions.hintContent: Recall the genetic, age, medication, and nutrition risk factors for skin disorders.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each client separately. Eliminate clients whose habits protect the skin.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client has applied an over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and then a friend's high-potency clobetasol cream to the face twice daily for 4 months to treat “redness.” Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible adverse effects of prolonged topical corticosteroid use? Select all that apply.
options: Thin, shiny skin on the treated areas
Small, visible blood vessels under the skin
Thickened, leathery plaques with exaggerated skin lines
Yellow, greasy scales on the eyebrows
Easy bruising in the treated areas
Hard, raised scar tissue extending past the original lesions
optionRationales: Correct. Long-term topical steroid use thins the skin.
Correct. As the skin thins, small blood vessels become visible.
Incorrect. Thickened, leathery skin comes from chronic scratching and rubbing. Steroids thin the skin rather than thicken it.
Incorrect. Greasy yellow scaling is a separate skin condition, not a steroid effect.
Correct. Thin skin with fragile vessels bruises easily.
Incorrect. Keloids are overgrown scars after skin injury, not a steroid effect.
questions.rationale: Prescription topical corticosteroids treat eczema, psoriasis, and dermatitis, but stronger products should not be used on the face, and long-term use can thin the skin. Thin skin shows visible vessels and bruises easily. The nurse teaches the client to stop using a friend's prescription and refers the client to the provider for a supervised plan.
questions.takeaway: Long-term topical steroids thin the skin: shiny skin, visible vessels, easy bruising.
questions.hintContent: Steroids reduce inflammation but also weaken the dermis over time. Think about what thin skin looks like.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each option separately. Exclude findings caused by a different process (chronic rubbing, abnormal scarring).

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Pharmacologic Therapy
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 17-year-old about starting benzoyl peroxide 5% gel for mild inflammatory acne. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?
options: “I'll scrub my face hard twice a day so the gel can soak in better.”
“I'll apply extra gel to a pimple that shows up before a big event.”
“If my skin gets dry and flaky, the medicine isn't working for me.”
“The gel can bleach fabric, so I'll use white towels.”
optionRationales: Harsh scrubbing irritates the skin and worsens inflammatory acne. A gentle cleanser is used.
Using more does not work faster. It increases irritation and dryness.
Mild dryness and peeling are expected early effects, not signs of treatment failure. The client can reduce frequency and use a noncomedogenic moisturizer.
Correct. Benzoyl peroxide is an oxidizing agent that bleaches hair, towels, and clothing.
questions.rationale: Benzoyl peroxide is a first-line OTC acne treatment. It kills Cutibacterium acnes and helps unplug follicles. Teaching includes gentle cleansing, a thin layer once daily at first and then increased as tolerated, expected dryness, bleaching of fabrics and hair, sun protection, and that improvement takes 6–8 weeks.
questions.takeaway: Benzoyl peroxide: gentle cleansing, a thin layer, expected dryness, and it bleaches fabric.
questions.hintContent: Recall how benzoyl peroxide works, its common expected side effects, and its effect on fabrics.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the statement that is true AND safe. Eliminate options with more is better thinking.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Lifespan Considerations – Infants and Children
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 7-year-old is brought to the school nurse with bright red cheeks that look like they were slapped and a lacy, pink rash on the arms. The child had a mild cold last week and is now afebrile and playful. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Chickenpox
Fifth disease
Roseola
Pityriasis rosea
optionRationales: Chickenpox causes itchy vesicles in crops, with lesions in different stages, not a slapped-cheek rash.
Correct. Fifth disease typically begins with mild cold symptoms, followed by a bright red “slapped cheek” rash and then a lacy rash on the arms and legs.
Roseola causes several days of high fever followed by a rash that appears as the fever breaks, usually in infants and toddlers.
Pityriasis rosea starts with a single larger oval “herald patch” and then smaller oval patches on the trunk.
questions.rationale: Fifth disease, roseola, and pityriasis rosea are childhood skin conditions listed with lifespan considerations. Fifth disease is recognized by its bright red “slapped cheek” rash followed by a lacy rash on the limbs. The nurse notifies the parent and refers the child to the provider for confirmation.
questions.takeaway: Slapped cheeks + lacy rash on the limbs = fifth disease.
questions.hintContent: Recall the distinctive appearance of each childhood rash condition.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the most distinctive cue in the stem (the cheeks) to the condition known for it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Lifespan Considerations – Infants and Children
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A 7-month-old has had frequent loose stools for 2 days. The nurse notes red, shiny, irritated skin on the buttocks and genitals where the diaper touches the skin, with the deep skin folds spared. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The infant's rash is most consistent with {0}, as evidenced by {1}. The nurse should teach the parent to {2}.

options: irritant diaper dermatitis
allergic contact dermatitis
impetigo
chickenpox
redness limited to skin exposed to stool and urine
honey-colored crusts
vesicles in different stages
a rash shaped like a metal snap
change diapers often and keep the skin clean and dry
scrub the area with antibacterial soap at each change
cover the area with plastic pants to hold in moisture
leave soiled diapers on longer so the skin can rest

questions.rationale: Infants have the strongest irritant response. Irritant contact dermatitis is non-immune damage from chemicals, and in the diaper area, stool and urine are the irritants. The rash is limited to exposed skin. Prevention and care are proper diaper care with frequent changes and keeping the skin clean and dry, without harsh cleansing.
questions.takeaway: Diaper rash from stool and urine = irritant dermatitis. Change often, keep clean and dry.
questions.hintContent: Recall which age group has the strongest irritant response and what irritates diapered skin.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the condition first, then choose evidence and teaching that match it.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Lifespan Considerations – Adolescents
questions.clientNeed: Psychosocial Integrity
questions.stem: A 16-year-old with dark brown skin has healing acne with dark spots where the pimples were. The teen says, “I hate how I look. I bought a strong skin-bleaching cream online, and I use it twice a day.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Those dark spots are permanent, so the bleaching cream is the only thing that may help.”
“Apply the cream only at night and in a thinner layer so it is less likely to irritate your skin.”
“That sounds hard. Bleaching creams can irritate skin. Let's ask your provider about safer options.”
“Try covering the spots with makeup instead, since acne is a normal part of being a teenager.”
optionRationales: Discoloration after lesions heal often fades over time with acne control and sun protection. This response is inaccurate and discourages the teen.
Changing the timing does not remove the risk of irritation or interactions from an unregulated product.
Correct. The nurse acknowledges the teen's feelings, explains the risks of bleaching creams, and refers for safe, effective treatment.
This dismisses the teen's concern about body image and does not address the unsafe product.
questions.rationale: Darker skin may show discoloration after lesions heal, and darker skin is more prone to inflammation. Adolescents often have acne, and skin changes deeply affect self-image. Some treatments, such as makeup and bleaching creams, can irritate the skin or interact with medications. The nurse addresses safety, acknowledges the teen's feelings, and supports safe options.
questions.takeaway: Dark marks after acne are common in darker skin. Stop unsafe bleaching creams and offer safe, respectful options.
questions.hintContent: Recall the skin concerns specific to darker skin tones and the risks of bleaching creams.
questions.hintStrategy: The best response addresses the safety issue AND the teen's feelings without false information or dismissal.

questions.ref: Module 21 · Tissue Integrity · Lifespan Considerations – Older Adults
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: An 81-year-old client in assisted living has dry, flaky, itchy skin on the legs and back with scratch marks. No rash or lesions are present. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Apply an alcohol-based lotion to cool the itchy areas
Use a mild, fragrance-free liquid cleanser instead of deodorant soap
Apply an emollient to damp skin immediately after bathing
Add a scented bath oil to hot bath water to relieve the itching
Keep the client's fingernails short and smooth
Keep the room humidity low to prevent mold growth
optionRationales: Incorrect. Alcohol-based products evaporate quickly and dry the skin further, which worsens xerosis and itching. Thick, fragrance-free emollients are used instead.
Correct. Harsh or deodorant soaps are alkaline and drying. Mild liquid cleansers protect the skin barrier.
Correct. Moisturizing damp skin right after bathing traps water in the stratum corneum.
Incorrect. Hot water and fragrances dry and irritate the skin, and bath oil makes the tub slippery, which increases fall risk.
Correct. Short, smooth nails reduce skin damage and infection risk from scratching.
Incorrect. Low humidity makes xerosis worse. A humidifier is recommended, especially in winter.
questions.rationale: Xerosis and pruritus are common in older adults because of reduced sebaceous and sweat gland activity and a thinner epidermis. Care focuses on bathing every other day with lukewarm water and mild cleansers, emollients on damp skin, avoiding drying or scented products, adequate humidity and fluids, and protecting fragile skin from scratching, while keeping safety in mind (falls).
questions.takeaway: Older adult dry skin: mild cleanser, lukewarm water, moisturize damp skin, no alcohol or scents, keep nails short.
questions.hintContent: Recall the age-related changes in sebaceous glands and the epidermis that cause xerosis.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option for whether it adds moisture and protects the skin without creating a safety hazard.
